title: 大秦景教流行中國碑 — the Da Qin Jingjiao stele of 781 describes 大秦國, citing the Illustrated Record of the Western Regions and the Han and Wei histories
language_note: Literary Chinese, cut on a limestone stele erected at Chang'an in 781 CE by the Church of the East in Tang China and unearthed at Xi'an in the early seventeenth century. The passage excerpted is not doctrine and not narrative: it is the monument's account of the country the church claimed as its homeland, written in the register of a Chinese geographical notice and openly citing Chinese sources for it.
date: 781 CE (建中二年). The excerpted passage describes 大秦國 in the present tense of the eighth century while citing Han- and Wei-period sources for it, so its testimony is 781 and its content is older.
findspot: Chang'an (Xi'an), Shaanxi. The stele is extant and now stands in the Beilin (Stele Forest) Museum, Xi'an.
original_text_excerpt: 案西域圖記及漢魏史策。大秦國南統珊瑚之海。北極眾寶之山。西望仙境花林。東接長風弱水。其土出火浣布．返魂香．明月珠．夜光璧。俗無寇盜。人有樂康。法非景不行。主非德不立。土宇廣濶。文物昌明。
original_text_note:
Verbatim Literary Chinese, 93 characters, CBETA T54n2144 lines 1289b18-1289b22, COPIED BY HAND from raw.githubusercontent.com/cbeta-org/xml-p5/master/T/T54/T54n2144.xml on 2026-09-01.

EDITORIAL ACTS, DECLARED. The <lb/> line-break elements are removed and the three words they split are closed up: 珊|瑚, 東接|長風 and 夜|光璧. Nothing else is altered. The ． separators in 火浣布．返魂香．明月珠．夜光璧 are U+FF0E FULLWIDTH FULL STOP and are the edition's own punctuation, kept rather than normalised to 、; 濶 in 土宇廣濶 is U+6FF6 and is the edition's character, not a variant introduced here. The curator's capture corrected this record's author, who had predicted 廣闊.

ONE CHARACTER IN THIS EXCERPT IS AN EMENDATION AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. The 浣 of 火浣布 carries a critical apparatus in the source file: <lem wit="#wit.cbeta">浣</lem> against <rdg wit="#wit.orig">綄</rdg>, CBETA's reading supported by cross-reference to T32n1675 and T48n2003. The excerpt carries 浣 because that is what the cited edition prints, and the witness reading is recorded here and in the reference_translation, which is the chunked field where a reader and a model can both see it.

THE BASE TEXT IS A RUBBING, which this record's author had wrongly written down as a book recension before the apparatus was captured. The Taishō note for this text reads 【原】拓本石田幹之助氏藏 — the base witness is a rubbing of the stone in the collection of Ishida Mikinosuke. So the transmission is stone → rubbing → Taishō → CBETA, and not a manuscript line liable to the recension problem F4_CANDIDATES records against Kanripo's Siku Quanshu base.
reference_translation:
According to the Illustrated Memoir of the Western Regions, and the historical books of the Han and Wei dynasties, the kingdom of Syria reaches south to the Coral Sea; on the north it joins the Gem Mountains; on the west it extends toward the borders of the immortals and the flowery forests; on the east it lies open to the violent winds and tideless waters. The country produces fire-proof cloth, life-restoring incense, bright moon-pearls, and night-lustre gems. Brigands and robbers are unknown, but the people enjoy happiness and peace. None but Illustrious laws prevail; none but the virtuous are raised to sovereign power. The land is broad and ample, and its literary productions are perspicuous and clear.

TWO PUBLISHED READINGS OF 大秦國, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME COUNTRY. Wylie, above, renders the three characters 'the kingdom of Syria'. James Legge, The Nestorian Monument of Hsî-an Fû (1888), p. 9, renders them 'the kingdom of Tâ Ts'in', the transliteration he uses throughout for the Roman Orient. The reading is disputed and this record does not settle it. That is not an evasion: the reason the passage is in this corpus is that a Tang Christian community claimed a homeland its neighbours called 大秦, and whether those characters name Rome, the Roman East, or Syria is the question the corpus is asking rather than an answer it holds.

AND THE TEXT IS NOT SETTLED AT ONE CHARACTER EITHER. The edition's apparatus prints 浣【CB】，綄【大】 — the 浣 of 火浣布, the asbestos or fire-proof cloth, is an emendation by CBETA supported against T32n1675 and T48n2003, while the witness rubbing reads 綄.
translation_source: Alexander Wylie, 'Inscription of the Nestorian Monument', in The Open Court, A Monthly Magazine, Volume XXIII (Chicago: The Open Court Publishing Company, 1909), p. 35; consulted at sacred-texts.com/journals/oc/inm.htm, a transcription reduced to HTML by Christopher M. Weimer, July 2002. THE CHAIN IS THREE STEPS AND IS NAMED RATHER THAN DRESSED UP: Wylie's translation, the 1909 Open Court reprint, and a 2002 hand transcription. It was preferred over Legge 1888 for a reason recorded in FINDING 53 — the only open Legge text is an OCR layer, and this English is a corrected transcription. The four words quoted from Legge in the reference_translation were read off the PAGE IMAGE of p. 9, not off that OCR.
reference_translation_note:
THE APOSTROPHE IN Tâ Ts'in IS A JUDGEMENT AND IS RECORDED AS ONE. It is written here as U+2019, the typographic form used throughout Legge's 1888 letterpress. The page scan does not distinguish U+2019 from U+0027 at the resolution available, and that exact substitution is the one FINDING 48 and FINDING 50 measured twice. The determination is the volume's typographic convention, not the pixels.

THE CIRCUMFLEX IS NOT A JUDGEMENT. The page prints Tâ Ts'in. The archive.org OCR prints Ta Ts'in, and so did the curator's first reading back from the page. Both capture paths dropped the same diacritic in the same direction, and the record has it only because they were checked against each other — FINDING 50's arrangement, measured a second time on four words.

WHAT THE ENGLISH IS NOT. Wylie's rendering decides, in its first clause, the question this record exists to hold open. A reader who takes 'the kingdom of Syria' as the corpus's position has been misled by the translation chunk, which is why Legge's reading sits three sentences later in the same chunk rather than in the notes, where the model would never see it.

F4 Part 2, record 33, and East Asia's third record carrying retrieval-eligible source-language text.

WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT ROME. A Christian community in Tang China, on a monument it erected in the imperial capital, describes the country it came from — and describes it by CITING CHINESE BOOKS: 案西域圖記及漢魏史策, 'according to the Illustrated Record of the Western Regions and the histories of the Han and Wei'. The bounds it gives are the Da Qin topoi this corpus already holds in eastasia-01-weilue and eastasia-02-hou-hanshu, and the products are the same list — asbestos cloth, soul-returning incense, bright-moon pearls, night-shining jade. The influence runs in an unexpected direction: to explain itself to a Chinese readership, a church of Roman origin reached not for its own memory of Rome but for the Chinese historians' Rome. The eleven characters of source-citation are the record, as much as the bounds are.

GLOSS-CAPABLE, DECLARED, and one of the two ruling 60 says F4 must deliver. Both halves are inside the chunked reference_translation and neither is in these notes, which the loader does not chunk — the trap gloss_capable_declared was added to make visible, and the way F3 lost its second gloss record. The alternative reading is 大秦國 as 'the kingdom of Syria' (Wylie) against 'the kingdom of Tâ Ts'in' (Legge); the statement that the reading is uncertain is the edition's own apparatus on 浣 against the witness 綄.

RULING 55, AND THIS RECORD MAKES ITS TEST HARDER RATHER THAN EASIER. The prediction registered before any East Asian candidate was examined is that both china-describes-rome pairs move down when F4's Literary Chinese records about Rome enter the index, and that weilue is likelier to leave the top 6. A Literary Chinese passage describing Da Qin's bounds and products, sharing vocabulary with both of those records, is the most direct competitor those pairs could have been given. The passage was chosen because Legge's uncertainty and the edition's apparatus are both here and nowhere else nearby — but choosing it sharpens the prediction, and that is written down before the run rather than claimed after it.

FINDING 53 governs how this record was captured. The English is not taken from archive.org's _djvu.txt, which is an OCR layer and was measured on this record dropping a diacritic and splicing a marginal note into the middle of a sentence. The four words quoted from Legge were read off the page image.

DECLARED, NOT RESOLVED IN THIS SESSION, on the same terms as record 32's Talmis: the id is written so ingest.gazetteer --check can accept or refuse it on its next run, and if it does not resolve against the cached snapshot the placement must be corrected or demoted to a regional ground. The findspot is the stele's own city and the record's argument depends on it — a monument about Rome standing in the Tang capital.

ROLE IS `focus`, NOT `findspot`. The vocabulary is closed -- A5 derives network edges from it -- and `findspot` is not in it. The first draft of this record invented the word, which is the closed vocabulary doing its job: a role the edge-builder cannot read would have dropped this place off the network without failing anything.

AND 大秦國 IS DELIBERATELY NOT PLACED. It is the only other place this passage names, and the record's whole gloss is that two published translators put it in two different countries. A gazetteer id for it would settle, in a field no reader argues with, exactly the question the reference_translation holds open -- and it would settle it silently, because a coordinate carries no apparatus. The absence is the claim, and it is the same argument ruling 54's unstamped pairs make one file over.
